slides.title: Your app is mostly other people's code
slides.summary: A typical frontend pulls in hundreds of packages. Any one of them can be vulnerable or malicious.
body: Most of the code in a modern bundle comes from node_modules. Attacks on that supply chain take a few forms:

ul: Known vulnerabilities in an old version of a library.
Compromised maintainers: a stolen npm token publishes a malicious version of a popular package.
Install scripts that run code on developer and CI machines during npm install.

body: <mark>Every dependency is code you ship with full access to your page. Add them as deliberately as you'd add your own code.</mark>

items.label: one compromised package
items.sub: runs in your users' browsers or your CI

slides.title: Keeping dependencies safe
slides.summary: Lock versions, audit continuously, update in small steps and limit what installs can do.

ul: Commit the lockfile and install with npm ci in CI, so builds use exactly the reviewed versions.
Audit: npm audit, Dependabot or Renovate flag known vulnerabilities and open update PRs.
Update often, in small steps, so a fix is never stuck behind a painful major upgrade.
Review new packages: maintenance, downloads, number of maintainers, install scripts, size.
Limit install scripts (--ignore-scripts where possible) and use a delay before adopting brand-new releases.

body.note: npm audit reports a lot of noise from dev-only tools. Triage by whether the vulnerable code actually ships to users or runs in CI.

code: npm audit --omit=dev     # what ships to users
